style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly. Transliterations are ASCII-normalized (lowercase, diacritics dropped) relative to the lexicon's spellings.
chapterNote: Chapter 13 is a string of antithetic proverbs that keep circling three linked themes: the mouth, the money, and the discipline that masters both. Again and again the wise son who takes correction is set against the scoffer who will not hear it (vv. 1, 13, 18, 24); guarded speech is set against reckless speech (vv. 2-3); honest, patient gain is set against wealth grabbed by fraud (vv. 7, 11, 22-23); and the bright, well-fed life of the righteous is set against the snuffed-out lamp and empty belly of the wicked (vv. 9, 25). The hinge of the chapter is verse 12 -- hope deferred and hope fulfilled -- which lifts the whole list above mere prudence into longing for the tree of life.

1.text: A wise son takes his father's correction to heart, but a mocker will not so much as listen when he is rebuked.
1.amp: A wise son [chakham -- skilled, discerning] heeds his father's instruction [musar -- corrective discipline, the shaping kind], but a scorner [luts -- the one who jeers at correction] does not listen [shama] to rebuke [gearah -- sharp reproof].
1.notes: musar (H4148) is formative correction, the loving discipline that shapes a son; luts (H3887) is the scoffer, the book's hardest case, who treats reproof as an insult. The contrast is not cleverness versus dullness but a teachable ear versus a closed one.

2.text: From the fruit of his mouth a man eats well, but the appetite of the treacherous feeds on violence.
2.amp: From the fruit of his mouth [peh -- speech, the lips' yield] a man eats good things [tov], but the soul [nephesh -- the craving inner self] of the treacherous [bagad -- the faithless, the betrayers] feeds on violence [chamas -- brutal wrong].
2.notes: the proverb plays on eating: words are a harvest the speaker himself must swallow. tov (H2896) is the wholesome fruit of good speech; chamas (H2555) is violent injustice, and the bagad (H898), the faithless, hunger for it. What a man speaks, he ends up feeding on.

3.text: Whoever guards his mouth keeps his life; the one who flings his lips wide open brings himself to ruin.
3.amp: He who guards [natsar -- keeps watch over] his mouth [peh] keeps [shamar -- preserves] his life [nephesh]; the one who opens wide his lips [saphah] comes to ruin.
3.notes: two sentry-verbs are doubled here -- natsar (H5341) and shamar (H8104) -- binding the guarding of the mouth to the guarding of the soul itself. Loose, unguarded speech is pictured as lips flung open like an unlatched gate, an invitation to destruction.

4.text: The sluggard craves and craves, yet has nothing; but the soul of the diligent is made rich and full.
4.amp: The soul [nephesh] of the sluggard [atsel -- the lazy man] longs [avah -- craves, yearns] and gets nothing, but the soul of the diligent [charuts -- the sharp, hard-working one] is made fat [dashen -- enriched, satisfied, prospered].
4.notes: the sluggard's tragedy is not that he lacks desire but that desire is all he has -- avah (H183) is real craving with no labor behind it. dashen (H1878) pictures the soul of the charuts (H2742), the diligent, made fat, the Hebrew image of full prosperity; wanting is not the same as working.

5.text: The righteous man hates a lying word, but the wicked acts shamefully and brings disgrace on himself.
5.amp: A righteous man [tsaddiq] hates [sane] a false word [sheqer -- deception, the lie], but the wicked [rasha] is loathsome and comes to shame [chapher -- is confounded, brought to disgrace].
5.notes: sheqer (H8267) is falsehood as a settled thing, a word built to deceive; the tsaddiq (H6662) does not merely avoid it but hates it. The wicked, by contrast, gives off a stench (the root H887) and ends in chapher (H2659), public shame -- his character betrayed by its own smell.

6.text: Righteousness stands guard over the one whose way is blameless, but wickedness topples the sinner.
6.amp: Righteousness [tsedaqah] guards [natsar -- keeps watch over] the one upright [tom -- whole, with integrity] in his way [derek], but wickedness [rishah] overthrows the sinner [chattath -- literally 'sin' itself].
6.notes: natsar (H5341) returns from v.3 -- now it is righteousness that mounts guard over the man of tom (H8537), wholeness without a hidden seam. The Hebrew names the sinner simply as 'sin' (chattath, H2403): a man's own rishah (H7564), wickedness, is the thing that knocks his legs out from under him.

7.text: One man pretends to be rich and has nothing at all; another plays the pauper, yet holds great wealth.
7.amp: There is one who makes himself rich [ashar] yet has nothing, and one who makes himself poor [rush -- plays at being destitute] yet has great [rav] riches [hon -- substance, real wealth].
7.notes: the proverb exposes the gap between show and substance. hon (H1952) is genuine wealth; the verse sets the man who inflates an empty purse against the man who hides a full one -- and quietly warns that appearances, in either direction, deceive.

8.text: A man's riches may buy back his life, but the poor man hears no rebuke -- not so much as a menacing word.
8.amp: The ransom [kopher -- the price paid to redeem a life] of a man's [ish] life [nephesh] is his riches, but the poor man [rush] hears [shama] no rebuke -- no threat at all.
8.notes: kopher (H3724) is ransom money, the sum that buys back a forfeited life. Wealth can be a shield -- and a target; the poor man's very emptiness leaves him nothing to extort, so no menacing voice comes for him. The proverb cuts both ways on the value of riches.

9.text: The light of the righteous burns bright and glad, but the lamp of the wicked is snuffed out.
9.amp: The light [or] of the righteous [tsaddiq] rejoices [samach -- shines gladly, burns merrily], but the lamp [ner] of the wicked [rasha] is put out.
9.notes: or (H216) is light itself, broad and steady; ner (H5216) is a single household lamp. The righteous have shining light that even seems to rejoice (samach, H8055), while the wicked have only a small flame -- and it is extinguished. To 'put out a man's lamp' is a Hebrew idiom for ending his line and his life (cf. Job 18:5-6).

10.text: Pride does nothing but breed quarrels, but wisdom belongs to those who will take advice.
10.amp: By pride [zadon -- arrogant insolence] comes [natan -- gives, gives rise to] only strife [matstsah -- contention, quarreling], but with those who take counsel [yaats -- the well-advised] is wisdom [chokmah].
10.notes: zadon (H2087) is overbearing arrogance, and the proverb makes it the sole parent of strife -- pride natan (H5414), gives rise to, nothing but matstsah (H4683), contention. Wisdom is found in the opposite posture: the willingness to be counseled (yaats, H3289). The teachable man of v.1 reappears here as the peaceable one.

11.text: Wealth got like a breath of vapor dwindles away, but the one who gathers it bit by bit, by honest labor, makes it grow.
11.amp: Wealth [hon] gained by vanity [hebel -- vapor, a breath, fraud that is here and gone] dwindles [maat -- is made small], but he who gathers [qabats] by hand -- by labor -- multiplies [rabah -- makes it many] it.
11.notes: hebel (H1892) is the 'vapor' word of Ecclesiastes -- wealth gotten by a puff of fraud is as fleeting as breath, and maat (H4591) shrinks it to nothing. The honest opposite is hand-by-hand gathering (qabats, H6908) that rabah (H7235), grows large by patience. Slow and clean outlasts fast and crooked.

12.text: Hope long deferred makes the heart sick, but a longing fulfilled is a tree of life.
12.amp: Hope [tochelet] deferred [mashak -- drawn out, dragged on] makes the heart [leb] sick [chalah -- weak, ailing], but the desire [taavah -- the longing] that comes is a tree [ets] of life [chay].
12.notes: mashak (H4900) is to drag or stretch out -- tochelet (H8431), hope, pulled long and thin until the leb (H3820), the heart, sickens (chalah, H2470). When the taavah (H8378) at last arrives, it is no small relief but a 'tree of life,' the Eden image (cf. Prov 3:18; 11:30) of flourishing, restored life. This verse is the emotional center of the chapter.

13.text: Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but the one who reveres the commandment will be rewarded.
13.amp: Whoever despises [buz -- holds in contempt] the word [dabar] will be destroyed, but he who fears [yare -- reveres, stands in awe of] the commandment [mitsvah] will be rewarded -- and kept in peace [shalam].
13.notes: buz (H936) is open contempt; to sneer at God's word is to pledge one's own ruin. The reward verb is shalam (H7999), built on shalom -- the marginal reading 'shall be in peace' is no accident: the one who reveres (yare, H3373) the command is paid back in wholeness and peace.

14.text: The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning a man away from the snares of death.
14.amp: The instruction [torah -- the teaching] of the wise [chakham] is a fountain [maqor -- spring, source] of life [chay], to turn aside [sur -- depart, swerve away] from the snares [moqesh -- traps, baited gins] of death [mavet].
14.notes: torah (H8451) here is the practical teaching of the wise, and maqor (H4726) is a living spring -- water that keeps a man alive. Its work is rescue: to make him sur (H5493), swerve clear, of the moqesh (H4170), the hidden death-traps. Wisdom is not decoration but survival.

15.text: Sound good sense wins favor, but the road of the treacherous never eases.
15.amp: Good [tov] understanding [sekel -- insight, prudence] gives favor [chen -- grace, goodwill], but the way [derek] of the treacherous [bagad -- the faithless] is hard [ethan -- harsh, unyielding, ever the same].
15.notes: sekel (H7922) is practical good sense, and it earns chen (H2580), the favor of God and men. ethan (H386) ordinarily means perennial or ever-flowing; applied to the road of the bagad (H898) it means relentless and rugged -- a way that never eases, the wearing hardness sin grinds into its own path.

16.text: Every prudent man acts out of knowledge, but a fool spreads his folly out for all to see.
16.amp: Every prudent man [arum -- shrewd, sensible] acts [asah] with knowledge [daat], but a fool [kesil -- the dull, stubborn fool] spreads open [paras -- unfolds, puts on display] his folly [ivvelet].
16.notes: arum (H6175) is the same 'shrewd' word used of the serpent in Eden, here turned to good: the prudent man thinks before he moves. The kesil (H3684) does the reverse -- paras (H6566), he unfurls his ivvelet (H200) like a banner, advertising the very foolishness he ought to hide.

17.text: A wicked messenger tumbles into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.
17.amp: A wicked [rasha] messenger [malak -- envoy, courier] falls [naphal] into harm [ra], but a faithful [emun -- trustworthy] ambassador is healing [marpe -- a cure, a making-well].
17.notes: in a world where word traveled only by courier, the messenger's character was everything. The unreliable malak (H4397) drops his charge into ra (H7451), trouble, while the envoy of emun (H529), faithfulness, becomes marpe (H4832), healing itself -- to those who sent him and those who receive him alike.

18.text: Poverty and disgrace come to the one who shrugs off discipline, but whoever takes correction to heart will be honored.
18.amp: Poverty [resh] and shame [qalon -- dishonor, disgrace] come to him who refuses [para -- lets loose, throws off] instruction [musar], but he who keeps [shamar -- heeds, holds onto] reproof [tokachat] will be honored [kabad -- weighted with honor].
18.notes: para (H6544) means to let loose or cast off restraint -- to refuse musar (H4148) is to throw discipline overboard, and resh (H7389), poverty, with qalon (H7036), disgrace, is the freight that washes back. The one who instead guards (shamar, H8104) reproof is kabad (H3513), made weighty with honor; in Hebrew, glory is heaviness.

19.text: A longing fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but fools find it loathsome to turn away from evil.
19.amp: A desire [taavah -- longing] accomplished [hayah -- come to be] is sweet [arev -- pleasant, agreeable] to the soul [nephesh], but it is an abomination [toevah -- a detestable thing] to fools [kesil] to turn aside [sur -- depart] from evil [ra].
19.notes: taavah (H8378) and sur (H5493) both echo v.12 and v.14, knitting the chapter together. The sweet thing, the arev (H6149) fulfillment of longing, lies on the far side of repentance -- but the kesil (H3684) finds the very turning from ra (H7451) a toevah (H8441), something he detests. He will not pay the one price that buys the sweetness.

20.text: Walk with the wise and you grow wise; keep company with fools and you come to harm.
20.amp: He who walks [halak] with the wise [chakham] becomes wise [chakam -- grows in wisdom], but a companion [raah -- one who keeps company, shepherds-with] of fools [kesil] will come to grief [rua -- to shout, raise a cry].
20.notes: the verse turns on sound: halak with the chakham makes one chakam -- the company you keep becomes the man you are. The tagged verb is rua (H7321), 'to shout, raise a cry'; the KJV margin's 'broken' reflects the traditional derivation from a look-alike root meaning to break, but the verb as tagged pictures the fool's companion ending in an outcry of grief. To herd with fools (the root raah, H7462, 'to associate') is to share their ruin. Character is contagious, for good or ruin.

21.text: Disaster dogs the steps of sinners, but the righteous are repaid with good.
21.amp: Evil [ra -- calamity, misfortune] pursues [radaph -- hunts, chases down] sinners [chatta], but to the righteous [tsaddiq] good [tov] shall be repaid [shalam -- made complete, paid in full].
21.notes: radaph (H7291) is the hunter's word -- calamity tracks the sinner like a pursuer who will not quit. The righteous meet the opposite reckoning: shalam (H7999), the same root as peace and recompense from v.13, pays them back in tov (H2896). Each is overtaken in the end by what he sowed.

22.text: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is stored away for the righteous.
22.amp: A good [tov] man leaves an inheritance [nachal -- bequeaths, hands down] to his children's children [ben], and the wealth [chayil -- substance, resources, strength] of the sinner [chote -- the one sinning] is laid up [tsaphan -- stored, treasured] for the just [tsaddiq].
22.notes: the good man's vision reaches past his own children to his grandchildren -- nachal (H5157) is a lasting bequest. The sinner here is the chote, the participle of chet (H2398), 'sin, trespass, offense' -- the one sinning. chayil (H2428) is amassed substance; and in God's economy it is tsaphan (H6845), quietly stored up -- the same 'treasure up' verb of 2:1 -- so that the sinner's hoard ends up in righteous hands (cf. Job 27:16-17; Eccl 2:26).

23.text: The fallow field of the poor could yield abundant food, but injustice sweeps it all away.
23.amp: Much [rob -- an abundance] food [okel] is in the freshly plowed land [niyr -- fallow ground, the poor man's tillage], but there is one swept away [saphah -- consumed, taken off] for want of justice [mishpat].
23.notes: niyr (H5215) is newly broken ground -- the poor man's small field can in fact grow plenty (rob, H7230). What ruins him is not bad soil but bad rulers: the absence of mishpat (H4941), justice, lets his harvest be saphah (H5595), swept off by oppression. Poverty is often robbery, not fate.

24.text: The one who withholds the rod hates his son, but the one who loves him is diligent to discipline him.
24.amp: He who withholds [chasak -- spares, holds back] his rod [shevet -- the staff of correction] hates [sane] his son [ben], but he who loves [ahab] him is diligent [shachar -- seeks early, attends at dawn] to discipline [musar] him.
24.notes: the proverb redefines love and hate by their fruit: to spare (chasak, H2820) the shevet (H7626) and let a child run uncorrected is, in the end, hatred. Real love is shachar (H7836) -- the word for seeking at first light, eager and timely -- applying musar (H4148) carefully and soon, before folly hardens. Discipline here is loving formation, not cruelty.

25.text: The righteous eats until his soul is satisfied, but the belly of the wicked goes empty.
25.amp: The righteous [tsaddiq] eats [akal] to the satisfying [soba -- fullness, his fill] of his soul [nephesh], but the belly [beten -- the gut, the innermost hunger] of the wicked [rasha] will want [chaser -- lack, be in need].
25.notes: the chapter that opened with eating one's words (v.2) closes with eating itself: the tsaddiq (H6662) is filled to satisfaction (soba, H7648), his nephesh content, while the rasha (H7563) is left with an empty beten (H990), forever short (chaser, H2637). The contrast is the whole book in miniature -- the righteous lack nothing they truly need; the wicked are never full.
